svg.title: Radiation dermatitis: three anchors and one crease
svg.desc: Schematic of the timeline and the site of radiation dermatitis. The timeline carries only the three anchors that have a source, and the figure adds no further detail. Anchor one, onset: the nursing guideline's defining sentence states the reaction usually appears 1 to 4 weeks after treatment starts. Anchor two, the peak: a prospective observation of 148 patients, mainly on conventional fractionation of 50 Gy in 25 fractions, found grade 2 reactions peaking at 61.9% two weeks after the end of treatment with grade 3 peaking at the same time at 8.3%, and across techniques and doses alike the peak fell 1 to 2 weeks after the end — so finishing treatment is not the end of it. Anchor three, settling: the guideline states the reaction can persist for several weeks afterwards, and the acute phase is defined as the first 90 days; the acute sub-study of a randomised trial found erythema after the one-week schedule settling about 2 weeks earlier than after the three-week schedule. Only one site is marked: the grading definition names grade 2 moist desquamation as mostly confined to skin folds and creases, which in breast radiotherapy means the axilla and the inframammary fold. No source specific to any other site was found, so no other site is marked. Who gets it worse also has sources: larger breast size raises the risk of moist desquamation as an independent factor in a randomised trial, and after mastectomy the addition of bolus to the chest wall gave a pooled grade 3 dermatitis rate of 9.6% across 27 studies against 1.2% without. The figure carries a red-line marker stating that two categories are not a self-care problem but a come-back-in problem: moist desquamation (broken skin, blistering, weeping) is flagged URGENT in the nursing guideline and requires medical attention within 24 hours — come back and let the team look at it rather than buying dressings and managing an open wound alone; and signs of infection mean coming back in, namely fever, foul odour, purulent discharge, and pain and swelling extending outside the treatment area, with rapidly worsening pain and a wound opening up belonging in the same category. A footnote gives the scale: taking radiotherapy at all sites together, about 90 to 95% of patients develop radiation dermatitis of some degree, the variable being severity.

g.text: SKIN — THREE ANCHORS, ONE PLACE
Radiation dermatitis: three anchors and one crease
Only three points on the timeline have a source: onset, peak, settling. A finer week-by-week script does not
exist in the literature, so this figure does not draw one.
Finishing treatment is not the end — the peak usually falls in the week or two after the last fraction.
Treatment starts
Treatment ends
Weeks 1 to 4: onset
About 2 weeks after the end: the peak
Settling over the following weeks
The nursing guideline's defining sentence:
the reaction usually appears 1 to 4 weeks
after treatment starts.
Prospective observation of 148 patients
(mainly conventional fractionation, 50 Gy
in 25 fractions): grade 2 reactions peaked
at 61.9% two weeks after the end, with
grade 3 peaking at the same time at 8.3%.
Across techniques and doses alike, the peak
fell 1 to 2 weeks after the end.
The guideline states the reaction can
persist for several weeks after
treatment; the acute phase is defined as
the first 90 days.
Erythema after the one-week schedule
settles about 2 weeks earlier than after
the three-week schedule (acute sub-study of
a randomised trial).
Where it breaks down first: the creases
Axilla
Inframammary fold
The grading definition names one place only: grade 2 moist desquamation
is 'mostly confined to skin folds and creases' — in breast
radiotherapy, that means the axilla and the inframammary fold.
Who gets it worse: larger breast size raises the risk of moist
desquamation (an independent factor in a randomised trial); after
mastectomy, adding bolus to the chest wall gave a pooled grade 3
dermatitis rate of 9.6% across 27 studies, against 1.2% without.
No source specific to any other site was found, so this figure marks
the creases only.
These two are not a self-care problem — they are a
come-back-in problem
Moist desquamation (broken skin, blistering, weeping) is flagged
URGENT in the nursing guideline: medical attention within 24 hours.
Come back and let us look at it; do not buy dressings and manage an
open wound yourself.
Signs of infection mean coming back in, not self-care: fever, foul
odour, purulent discharge, and pain and swelling extending outside
the treatment area. Rapidly worsening pain and a wound opening up
belong here too.
Say so at the next session if anything is getting worse — you see
the treatment team every day during the course, and that is the
safety net built into it.
The scale of it: taking radiotherapy at all sites together, about 90 to 95% of patients develop radiation dermatitis of some degree — the variable is severity,
not whether it happens.
Schematic, redrawn from the BC Cancer symptom management guideline on radiation dermatitis, Drost 2018, Brunt 2016 (FAST-Forward acute
sub-study), Pignol 2008 and Zasadziński 2022
Peak figures come from a mainly conventionally fractionated cohort; the grade-to-action pairing follows the guideline's own wording
